profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a university-affiliated epilepsy technology lab evaluating a draft protocol for the next iteration of a wearable seizure-detection device program. The team is using findings from a recent systematic review on user involvement in epilepsy medical device development to judge whether their current development plan adequately incorporates people with epilepsy, caregivers, and clinicians before submitting the protocol to the hospital's device innovation committee. The agenda is to review whether the proposal's user-involvement section is 'review-ready,' confirm which development stages are covered, assess whether the planned feedback activities are sufficient, and decide what revisions are needed before approval. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on submitting the protocol with minor edits versus sending it back for additional design work.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: Epilepsy device development, ambulatory EEG workflows, clinician-facing validation studies
members.background: A neurologist-engineer who leads translational epilepsy device projects at an academic medical center and has previously taken seizure-monitoring prototypes through pilot clinical evaluations.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol cleared this week so the project can stay aligned with a pending grant milestone, and she is trying to preserve the existing timeline without appearing dismissive of user-centered design.
hidden_assumptions: If end users have already shaped device requirements in earlier interviews, the current design review only needs to verify that their prior input is reflected rather than reopen major design questions.
When discussing 'users,' clinician and technician operational feedback can stand in for practical issues that patients and caregivers would otherwise raise at this stage.
A plan counts as covering the development process if user input is represented across concept, prototyping, and pre-clinical evaluation, even if manufacturing preparation is not addressed.
A protocol is 'review-ready' once the committee can see a defensible user-involvement rationale and concrete activities, even if recruitment materials and session logistics are still being finalized.

members.name: Elena Morales
members.role: Patient Engagement and Human Factors Specialist
members.expertise: Participatory design in medical devices, usability studies, caregiver and patient advisory methods
members.background: A human factors researcher with experience running co-design sessions for neurology and home-monitoring technologies in both academic and commercial settings.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol to establish a stronger participatory-design standard for the lab and is trying to secure meaningful involvement from people with epilepsy and caregivers without sounding like she is blocking progress.
hidden_assumptions: User involvement in a design review means current, direct engagement with people with epilepsy and caregivers on the actual near-final prototype and workflow, not only reliance on earlier studies.
When a team says 'users,' it primarily means the people living with the device at home and the caregivers supporting them, while clinicians are a separate stakeholder group.
A development plan only truly covers the process if it addresses what happens when the design moves toward production constraints such as packaging, training materials, and deployment realities.
A proposal is not 'review-ready' unless the participant-facing details are operational enough that the planned sessions could be scheduled immediately without redesigning the engagement approach.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the protocol has strong 'user involvement' and discuss strengthening the 'user voice.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the proposal incorporates user-related input broadly, including prior patient interviews from an earlier phase plus planned clinician and EEG-technician walkthroughs in this review cycle.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means direct involvement of people with epilepsy and caregivers in evaluating the current prototype and workflow during this design-review phase.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is normatively positive and widely used in the literature, so each assumes the other shares the common-sense meaning; because both support involvement in principle, nothing sounds contradictory on the surface.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the plan covers the 'full development process'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the protocol as covering 'the development process' or 'the stages we need right now.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the relevant scope for this review as concept refinement through pilot evaluation, consistent with the lab's pre-commercial remit; production-related considerations are outside this design review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the review should also account for downstream production-adjacent elements that affect real-world use, such as packaging language, onboarding, and handoff into deployment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing stage coverage at a high level and using the same lifecycle language from the systematic review, but each silently draws the project boundary in a different place that feels obvious for their role.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the protocol is 'review-ready' for committee submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes it is review-ready if the protocol contains enough rationale, a user-involvement plan, and placeholders for operational details that can be finalized after committee feedback.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes it is review-ready only if the recruitment approach, participant mix, session format, and user-facing materials are sufficiently specified to execute without redesign.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In academic medical device work, many teams use 'review-ready' loosely to mean ready for the next governance step, so both can say 'almost there' while holding different thresholds for completeness.

misalignment_points.topic: Which prior evidence counts as the 'earlier interviews'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both reference 'the earlier interviews' as support for keeping the current protocol lean.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 2022 semi-structured interviews with epilepsy nurses and EEG technologists that informed alert triage and dashboard layout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the 2023 home-use interviews with adults with epilepsy and two caregivers about wearability, stigma, and nighttime charging.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both datasets are genuinely earlier interview work on the same program, and both are salient to user-centered design, so the shorthand sounds perfectly coherent even though the underlying evidence base differs.

turns.inner_thought: I need to get this over the line today if possible. For committee purposes, the protocol is basically ready: the rationale is there, the user-involvement section is defensible, and the operational pieces can be tightened after we get the committee's read. I just need Elena to feel heard without reopening the schedule.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. My hope today is that we treat this as the final design review for the seizure-detection protocol and leave with a version that's review-ready for committee submission, ideally with only minor edits.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want to sound like I'm slowing things down, but I need the document to show real participatory design rather than just a general nod to it. If we're invoking the systematic review, then user involvement has to be visible in the current phase, not just inherited from older work.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I mainly want to be sure the proposal clearly shows strong user involvement and that the user voice is reflected in a way that's consistent with what the systematic review highlights for epilepsy devices.

turns.inner_thought: We already have what we need: the earlier interviews informed the dashboard and triage flow, and the upcoming clinician and EEG-tech walkthroughs will verify the prototype is still on track. That covers the development process for this stage. I shouldn't let this drift into a new round of broad redesign questions.
turns.utterance: I think we're actually in a good place on that. The development process is already well covered because we can point to the earlier interviews, and then in this cycle we're adding walkthroughs on the current prototype so the user involvement is visible in the draft.

turns.inner_thought: I'm glad she agrees on the principle. But the earlier interviews I'm thinking of were about home use, stigma, charging, and day-to-day realities, so I'd like that same user voice brought into the near-final workflow rather than treating the older data as sufficient by itself.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think that will land well if the user voice is also easy to see in the near-final home workflow. The earlier interviews brought up a lot of practical use concerns, so I'd like the user involvement language to make that continuity really clear.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, I can give a little ground as long as we don't expand beyond what this review needs. The committee doesn't expect us to solve packaging and deployment; they want to know the concept-to-pilot path is sound. And again, review-ready doesn't mean every logistical detail is locked.
turns.utterance: That should be fine. My view is that the committee mostly needs to see that the protocol spans the stages we need right now and that it's review-ready as a design-review document, without trying to solve everything at once.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with keeping it concise, but if the development process is supposed to feel complete, we should at least nod to the things that shape home adoption later. Otherwise it reads too lab-centered and not grounded in real use.
turns.utterance: Agreed, we don't need to overbuild it. I would just add a short section so the development process feels complete from a user perspective—something that acknowledges onboarding materials and packaging language without making the protocol much heavier.

turns.inner_thought: Best path is to keep this lean and lean on prior evidence. If we cite the earlier interviews more clearly and frame the walkthroughs as confirmation, we preserve the timeline and show continuity. No need to launch additional activities before submission.
turns.utterance: I can work with that. I'd still prefer to keep the protocol lean by citing the earlier interviews more explicitly and using the upcoming walkthroughs to confirm that the design direction still holds, rather than expanding the activities too much.

turns.inner_thought: As long as 'users' doesn't get flattened into staff perspectives. The earlier interviews I have in mind surfaced barriers that only people living with the device and caregivers would notice, so the draft needs to show that those voices are represented in this phase.
turns.utterance: That works for me as long as the protocol makes clear how people with epilepsy and caregivers will be represented in the user involvement plan. The earlier interviews identified day-to-day barriers that other stakeholders wouldn't necessarily see.

turns.inner_thought: We're close enough. I don't want 'representation' to become a demand for a whole new recruitment stream before committee. The draft is review-ready in substance, and the session logistics and materials can be filled in once we have approval to proceed.
turns.utterance: Understood. From my side, the draft is essentially review-ready now. I think the remaining details on session logistics and materials can be tightened after the committee confirms the direction, as long as the user-involvement rationale is clear in the submission.

turns.inner_thought: I can support submission, but only if the engagement piece is concrete enough that we could actually schedule sessions without rethinking the plan. Otherwise 'review-ready' is doing too much work. I need at least the participant mix and format nailed down in the document.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable submitting if we first make the participant mix and session format explicit enough that the user involvement plan reads as actionable rather than aspirational. Then it will feel genuinely review-ready to me.

turns.inner_thought: That's a manageable framing. I'll summarize this in the narrowest way possible: sharpen the citations to the earlier interviews, add one paragraph on home-use considerations, and tighten the section. If I keep it bounded, we can still submit this week.
turns.utterance: Okay, so the edits would be: clarify the earlier interviews, add a brief paragraph on home-use considerations, and tighten the user-involvement section so it's more concrete without expanding scope too much. That still keeps the stages we need right now in view.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll revise it in a way that makes the full user journey more visible, including the downstream touchpoints that matter for real-world use, and make the engagement plan operational enough to schedule. Maya seems aligned, so hopefully this sets a better standard without turning into a fight.
turns.utterance: Yes, that sounds workable. I'll revise the draft this afternoon so it reads as review-ready and is visibly grounded in the full user journey we've been discussing.
